movements.name: Psychedelic Poster
movements.summary: Dance-hall posters that bent Art Nouveau lettering and vibrating colour into a slow-to-read image you had to stop and decode.

principles.name: Legibility as a delay
principles.idea: Lettering swells to fill every gap in the shape it occupies, so reading becomes a deliberate act that holds the viewer in front of the poster.
principles.example: Wes Wilson, Bill Graham Presents poster 'Fly 8 Miles High with Me', 1966

principles.name: Vibrating complements
principles.idea: Equal-value complementary colours placed edge to edge make the boundary shimmer, so the flat print appears to move.
principles.example: Victor Moscoso, Neon Rose #2 poster for the Matrix, 1967

principles.name: Borrowed ornament, new body
principles.idea: Secession and Art Nouveau letterforms and Mucha-style figures are lifted wholesale and re-inked in fluorescent colour for a new audience.
principles.example: Wes Wilson, Family Dog poster 'Sin Dance', 1966

principles.name: The poster as merchandise
principles.idea: Event bills were reprinted and sold as wall art, turning ephemeral promotion into a collectible product and a style that could be licensed.

keyWorks.title: Neon Rose series for the Matrix

movements.name: Punk and Post-punk Graphics
movements.summary: Cut-up, photocopied, deliberately crude graphics for the punk explosion, and the cool modernist sleeves of the post-punk labels that followed.

principles.name: Ransom-note lettering
principles.idea: Letters cut from newspaper headlines and pasted at mismatched sizes make the message look illicit and anonymous, made with scissors rather than a typesetter.
principles.example: Jamie Reid, 'God Save the Queen' sleeve for the Sex Pistols, 1977

principles.name: Détournement of icons
principles.idea: An official image is defaced just enough to invert its meaning: the Queen's jubilee portrait with the eyes and mouth torn out.
principles.example: Jamie Reid, 'God Save the Queen' poster, 1977

principles.name: The sleeve as a puzzle
principles.idea: Packaging carries deliberate errors, die-cuts, misregistration and hidden codes, so the object rewards close attention and insider knowledge.
principles.example: Barney Bubbles, Elvis Costello 'This Year's Model' sleeve, deliberately miscropped, 1978

principles.name: Modernism as a found object
principles.idea: Post-punk designers quote Tschichold, scientific plots and classical paintings with cool detachment, placing the band name small or not at all.

keyWorks.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols

movements.name: New Wave Typography
movements.summary: Swiss typography taken apart from inside: Weingart's Basel classroom kept the grid's discipline and broke its rules, and his students carried it to America.

principles.name: Break the grid from inside
principles.idea: Start from Swiss order, then stair-step, letterspace, rotate and overlap type so the structure is visible precisely because it is being violated.

principles.name: Film as a layer
principles.idea: Halftone screens, typesetting film and photographs are sandwiched and re-photographed, so texture and transparency become typographic material.

principles.name: Type in deep space
principles.idea: Letters, colour swatches and photographs float at different apparent depths, a layered space rather than a flat page.
principles.example: April Greiman and Jayme Odgers, CalArts poster, 1978

principles.name: Readability over legibility
principles.idea: Instead of maximising letter recognition, the designer asks whether the whole composition draws a reader in and holds them.
principles.example: Dan Friedman, teaching at Yale and SUNY Purchase, 1969-1975

keyWorks.title: LA Summer Games runner poster (with Jayme Odgers)
Design Quarterly 133: Does It Make Sense?

movements.name: Memphis
movements.summary: Sottsass's Milan collective made furniture out of cheap laminate, clashing colour and toy-like geometry to mock good taste and functionalist restraint.

principles.name: Cheap material, luxury price
principles.idea: Printed plastic laminate, the material of diners and kitchens, is applied to gallery furniture so status and taste are put in question.

principles.name: Pattern as surface, not ornament
principles.idea: A squiggle or speckle covers a form flatly and arbitrarily, unrelated to structure, making the surface a graphic layer.
principles.example: Ettore Sottsass, Bacterio laminate pattern, used on Memphis pieces from 1981

principles.name: Object as character
principles.idea: A bookcase or lamp is composed like a totem or a figure, with arms and a head, so it reads as personality before function.

principles.name: Clash on purpose
principles.idea: Colours and shapes that should not sit together are stacked: pastel with black, terrazzo with primary yellow.

keyWorks.title: Valentine typewriter (with Perry A. King, Olivetti)

movements.name: Postmodern Typography
movements.summary: American and British designers read literary theory and the commercial vernacular into layouts that ask to be read in layers, not decoded once.

principles.name: Reading and seeing at once
principles.idea: Text is set to be both read and looked at: images and words interleave so meaning is assembled by the reader rather than delivered.
principles.example: Katherine McCoy, Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster, 1989

principles.name: Learn from the vernacular
principles.idea: Hand-lettered signs, clip art, Letraset and trade printing are treated as sources equal to Swiss modernism.
principles.example: Ed Fella, Detroit Focus Gallery poster 'Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision', 1987

principles.name: The designer as author
principles.idea: The designer adds a voice to the content rather than serving it invisibly, through self-initiated work, editing and commentary.
principles.example: Tibor Kalman, M&Co, Talking Heads '(Nothing But) Flowers' typographic video, 1988

principles.name: Theory as a design tool
principles.idea: Semiotics and post-structuralist ideas about how texts mean are tested directly in layout, and documented as a programme.
principles.example: Katherine and Michael McCoy, Cranbrook Design: The New Discourse, 1991

keyWorks.title: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster
Detroit Focus Gallery poster, Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision
Remain in Light (Talking Heads), with M&Co

movements.name: Emigre and Early Digital Type
movements.summary: A Berkeley magazine and foundry that designed type on and for the first Macintosh, then made the pages a public argument about legibility.

principles.name: Design for the machine's grain
principles.idea: Instead of forcing old typefaces into coarse screens and printers, letters are drawn from the pixel grid itself and its limits become the style.
principles.example: Zuzana Licko, Oakland (later Lo-Res), used in Emigre #3, 1985

principles.name: You read best what you read most
principles.idea: Legibility is learned habit, not a property of letterforms, so unfamiliar type is a question of exposure.

principles.name: The magazine as specimen
principles.idea: A publication shows its own foundry's fonts in use, and the fonts fund the magazine: medium, catalogue and business in one.
principles.example: Emigre magazine with Emigre Fonts, from 1985

principles.name: Distortion as a typeface
principles.idea: Typefaces encode accident, overlap and imperfection into the font file so any user can set 'damaged' type.
principles.example: Barry Deck, Template Gothic, drawn 1989, released by Emigre 1991

keyWorks.title: Emigre: Graphic Design into the Digital Realm

movements.name: Grunge Typography
movements.summary: Layered, distressed, intuitive layouts made with QuarkXPress and Photoshop, where texture and attitude carried music and youth-culture content.

principles.name: Intuition over system
principles.idea: Each spread is composed by eye and mood, not from a master grid; consistency is in attitude, not in measurements.

principles.name: Text as image
principles.idea: Body copy is cropped, overlapped, set in dingbats or run off the page when its texture says more than its words.
principles.example: David Carson, Bryan Ferry interview set in Zapf Dingbats, Ray Gun, 1990s

principles.name: Corporate language turned on itself
principles.idea: Logos, slogans and manuals are parodied into an invented corporation's identity.
principles.example: The Designers Republic, packaging and identity for Wipeout, 1995

principles.name: Type with a grudge
principles.idea: Typefaces carry political names and historical baggage so their form and title argue with the reader.

movements.name: Neo-modernist Revival
movements.summary: Designers in Amsterdam and Zurich returned to grids, grotesques and black-and-white after grunge, treating modernism as a critical language, not a corporate one.

principles.name: Helvetica as a found material
principles.idea: A neutral grotesque is used without irony and without decoration, so meaning comes from scale, rhythm and repetition alone.
principles.example: Experimental Jetset, John & Paul & Ringo & George T-shirt, 2001

principles.name: The responsive identity
principles.idea: A mark is a system that changes shape to fit its context instead of a fixed logo.
principles.example: Experimental Jetset, Whitney Museum 'Responsive W' identity, 2013

principles.name: The book as architecture
principles.idea: Scale, thickness, edges and binding are designed as carefully as the pages, so the object itself carries the content.

principles.name: Construct the letter
principles.idea: Typefaces are rebuilt from first principles and rules, a modernist method producing deliberately odd results.

figures.name: Wes Wilson
figures.summary: The Fillmore's poster artist, who adapted Secession lettering into the melting 'psychedelic' letterform that defined the San Francisco poster.

principles.name: Fill the shape
principles.idea: Letters stretch and swell until they fill a silhouette entirely, so the word becomes a shape before it becomes a word.
principles.example: Bill Graham Presents poster 'Fly 8 Miles High with Me', 1966

principles.name: Stop the passer-by
principles.idea: Lettering is built to be 'something people had to stop to figure out', making slowness the hook.
principles.example: Family Dog poster 'The Quick and the Dead', 1966

principles.name: Learn from Vienna
principles.idea: He took the block lettering of the Secession, notably Alfred Roller, and resculpted it rather than inventing from nothing.

keyWorks.title: Fly 8 Miles High with Me (Bill Graham Presents)

figures.name: Victor Moscoso
figures.summary: The one Yale-trained artist among the San Francisco poster makers, who turned Albers's colour theory into posters that vibrate.

principles.name: Colour as motion
principles.idea: Albers's lesson that adjacent colours change each other is applied at full saturation so the poster appears to flicker.

principles.name: Invert the academy
principles.idea: Trained at Cooper Union and Yale, he used that training against itself: academic colour and lettering skill applied to make posters harder to read, not easier.

principles.name: Sequence and loop
principles.idea: His comics repeat frames on a fixed grid so a story can be entered at any panel and read as a cycle.

keyWorks.title: Neon Rose series for the Matrix

figures.name: Peter Max
figures.summary: The New York illustrator who turned the 'Cosmic '60s' look into mass-licensed merchandise, posters and a Life magazine cover.

principles.name: The full spectrum
principles.idea: Rainbow gradients and Day-Glo colour, often the whole visible spectrum in one image, carry optimism directly.

principles.name: Style as licence
principles.idea: A single recognisable manner is applied across posters, clocks, clothing and stamps, making the artist a brand.

figures.name: Jamie Reid
figures.summary: The Sex Pistols' designer, who brought Situationist-style détournement and ransom-note lettering from a radical press into the record shop.

principles.name: Ransom note
principles.idea: Headline letters cut from newspapers and glued at random sizes make every word look stolen and every message anonymous.
principles.example: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols, 1977

principles.name: Deface the official image
principles.idea: A sanctioned portrait is altered just enough to turn it against itself.
principles.example: 'God Save the Queen' sleeve, from a Cecil Beaton photograph, 1977

principles.name: Graphics as agitation
principles.idea: Design comes from a political press, not an agency; the sleeve continues the pamphlet.

keyWorks.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols

figures.name: Barney Bubbles
figures.role: Graphic designer, art director, video director
figures.summary: Swiss-trained, mostly uncredited sleeve designer for Hawkwind, Stiff and Elvis Costello, who treated all of design history as a palette.

principles.name: History as a palette
principles.idea: Constructivism, Kandinsky, Pop and 1950s packaging are quoted freely, each chosen to say something about the record.
principles.example: Nick Lowe, Labour of Lust 'Hamer & sickle' logo, 1979

principles.name: Errors on purpose
principles.idea: Miscropping, wrong photographs and erratum stickers are designed in, rewarding the fan who notices.
principles.example: The Damned, Damned Damned Damned sleeve with deliberate wrong photo, 1977

principles.name: The sleeve as a kit
principles.idea: Fold-outs, die-cut postcards and build-it pyramids make the package an object to handle and assemble.

principles.name: Anonymity
principles.idea: From 1973 he mostly left his name off the work or used pseudonyms, so the band and the idea stayed in front.

figures.name: Peter Saville
figures.summary: Factory Records' co-founder and designer, who answered punk's mess with Tschichold, scientific plots and appropriated paintings.

principles.name: The cool answer to punk
principles.idea: He took the restrained New Typography of Tschichold as a parallel to the new wave coming out of punk.

principles.name: Appropriate and recontextualise
principles.idea: An image from another field (a pulsar plot, a Fantin-Latour still life) is lifted whole and made to stand for a record.

principles.name: Withhold the name
principles.idea: Band names and titles are small, coded or absent, so the sleeve reads as an artwork and the fan has to know.
principles.example: New Order, Blue Monday die-cut sleeve, 1983

figures.name: Neville Brody
figures.role: Graphic designer, art director, type designer
figures.summary: Art director of The Face, who drew custom geometric headline type and then founded FUSE to make type itself experimental.

principles.name: Draw the headline
principles.idea: Instead of buying display type, he drew constructivist-influenced alphabets for each magazine, so the publication's voice was its letterforms.

principles.name: The page as a poster
principles.idea: Magazine pages are composed like posters, with type rotated, scaled and used as image.

principles.name: Type as experiment
principles.idea: A publication ships new, often unusable fonts with essays, to treat typography as research rather than product.

figures.name: Wolfgang Weingart
figures.summary: The Basel teacher who took Swiss typography as a starting point and 'blew it apart', and whose students carried New Wave to America.

principles.name: Start from Swiss, then question it
principles.idea: Keep the base of Swiss typography (sans serif, asymmetry, the grid) and test every one of its rules to destruction.

principles.name: Typography as craft experiment
principles.idea: Letterspacing, stepped lines and reversed type are explored by hand in hot metal and film, so experiment stays physical.

principles.name: Teach, don't impose
principles.idea: He insisted he never forced a style on students; the 'Weingart style' was what students picked up and spread.
principles.example: Weiterbildungsklasse, Basel School of Design, from 1968

figures.name: April Greiman
figures.summary: Weingart's student who brought Basel New Wave to Los Angeles and was among the first to make the Macintosh a design medium.

principles.name: Objects in space
principles.idea: Type, swatches, lines and photographs float in a layered, illusionistic depth instead of sitting on the flat page.

principles.name: Use the crude tool
principles.idea: Low-resolution video capture and early Mac bitmaps are embraced as expressive material, not apologised for.
principles.example: Design Quarterly 133: Does It Make Sense?, 1986

principles.name: Hybrid imagery
principles.idea: Photography, video and type are fused into a single image so the medium boundaries disappear.

keyWorks.title: Design Quarterly 133: Does It Make Sense?

figures.name: Dan Friedman
figures.summary: Ulm- and Basel-trained designer and teacher who carried Weingart's ideas into American classrooms and argued for a 'radical modernism'.

principles.name: Readability, not legibility
principles.idea: He replaced legibility, a property of letters, with readability, whether a whole piece invites reading.

principles.name: Radical modernism
principles.idea: Keep modernism's social optimism but drop its puritan restraint, letting in colour, kitsch and the personal.

principles.name: No border between disciplines
principles.idea: Corporate identity, Day-Glo furniture and art catalogues are one practice.

figures.name: Ettore Sottsass
figures.summary: Olivetti's designer who brought colour and play to office machines, then founded Memphis to attack good taste head on.

principles.name: Bring the office into pop culture
principles.idea: A typewriter is coloured, named and marketed like a toy or a fashion item instead of equipment.
principles.example: Valentine typewriter, with Perry A. King, 1969

principles.name: Refuse the consumerist product
principles.idea: Objects become sculptural statements that question consumption rather than serve it.

principles.name: Radical, funny, outrageous
principles.idea: Design is made to provoke and amuse, against prevailing 'good taste'.

figures.name: Katherine McCoy
figures.summary: Co-chair of Cranbrook's design programme from 1971 to 1995, who joined Unimark-trained rigour to vernacular, semiotics and deconstruction.

principles.name: Layered reading
principles.idea: Visual and verbal readings overlap so a poster offers several routes in rather than one hierarchy.
principles.example: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster, 1989

principles.name: Studio as laboratory
principles.idea: Minimal assignments and weekly critiques let each student develop a personal design voice, balanced by real client work.

principles.name: Read deeply, then design
principles.idea: Students read history and theory behind their concerns and design with those ideas, from Venturi to post-structuralism.

keyWorks.title: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster

figures.name: Ed Fella
figures.summary: A Detroit commercial artist for thirty years who made exuberantly 'wrong' hand-built typography for gallery flyers, then taught a generation at CalArts.

principles.name: Use every tool at once
principles.idea: Found type, Letraset, stencils, scribble, clip art and the photostat sit together on one page.
principles.example: Detroit Focus Gallery poster, Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision, 1987

principles.name: Make every letter different
principles.idea: A sans serif is redrawn by hand with varying weights, curves and tails so no two characters repeat.

principles.name: After the fact
principles.idea: Posters made for those who attended an event, not to sell it beforehand, free the work from commercial persuasion.

keyWorks.title: Detroit Focus Gallery poster, Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision

figures.name: Rudy VanderLans
figures.summary: Dutch-trained founder, editor and designer of Emigre magazine, who made it the main forum for, and against, digital-era graphic design.

principles.name: The magazine as forum
principles.idea: A design magazine publishes argument as well as work, inviting guest editors and critics, including opponents.

principles.name: Specimen as design work
principles.idea: The type specimen is a designed artefact that makes you want the face and then shows how to use it.

principles.name: Change format with purpose
principles.idea: The magazine shrank from tabloid to letter size, to CD booklet, to book, as its content shifted from image to text.

keyWorks.title: Emigre: Graphic Design into the Digital Realm

figures.name: Zuzana Licko
figures.summary: Co-founder of Emigre Fonts, who drew the first Macintosh bitmap faces from the pixel up, then remade Baskerville and Bodoni for the digital page.

principles.name: Start from the constraint
principles.idea: Coarse screens and dot-matrix printers dictate the letter; the font is designed for 72 dots per inch rather than forced from metal.

principles.name: Legibility is habit
principles.idea: 'You read best what you read most': familiarity, not form, makes type readable.

principles.name: Revival as reinterpretation
principles.idea: A historical model is reworked for new uses, with a low x-height and abundant ligatures rather than a faithful copy.

figures.name: David Carson
figures.summary: A former pro surfer whose layouts for Beach Culture and Ray Gun made intuitive, layered, barely legible typography a mainstream style.

principles.name: Don't mistake legibility for communication
principles.idea: A page that is hard to read can still communicate, through texture and emotion, if it is honest to its content.

principles.name: Basic decisions make the work
principles.idea: Image choice, cropping and type choice matter more than the software's ability to overlap or fade.

principles.name: Each page its own answer
principles.idea: No template: every spread is resolved from scratch by intuition.

keyWorks.title: Nine Inch Nails, The Fragile packaging

figures.name: Jonathan Barnbrook
figures.summary: Type designer and activist who gives fonts provocative names, uses détournement against corporations, and designed Bowie's late sleeves.

principles.name: Design as a weapon
principles.idea: Graphic work is a political response, often parodying advertising's own language.
principles.example: Billboard 'Designers, stay away from corporations that want you to lie for them', 2001

principles.name: The loaded typeface
principles.idea: A font's name and its historical form (blackletter, inscription) carry an argument.

principles.name: Type as the cover
principles.idea: A bespoke typeface does the work of the image on a record sleeve.

figures.name: Tibor Kalman
figures.summary: Founder of M&Co and editor of Benetton's Colors, the 'bad boy' who used vernacular graphics and provocation as design's conscience.

principles.name: Vernacular against corporate
principles.idea: The language of cheap signs, menus and diners is used as a protest against corporate International Style.

principles.name: Good design needs a good client
principles.idea: Design is only good if it serves an ethical end and increases public awareness.

principles.name: Provoke with the obvious
principles.idea: A single doctored image, the Queen recast as Black, says more than an essay.
principles.example: Colors issue on race with doctored portraits, 1993

keyWorks.title: Talking Heads, Remain in Light (with the band)

figures.name: Stefan Sagmeister
figures.summary: An M&Co alumnus whose handmade, often bodily typography for music and his own lectures made the designer's life part of the content.

principles.name: The hand over the font
principles.idea: Lettering is cut, built or written physically, so the labour and risk of making show.
principles.example: AIGA Detroit lecture poster, text cut into his skin, 1999

principles.name: Hide and reveal
principles.idea: Packaging uses coloured cases and transparency so the image changes when you take it apart.
principles.example: Lou Reed, Set the Twilight Reeling, 1996

principles.name: Design about your own life
principles.idea: Personal maxims and experiments become public typography and exhibitions.
principles.example: Things I Have Learned in My Life So Far, 2008

keyWorks.title: Lou Reed, Set the Twilight Reeling
Things I Have Learned in My Life So Far

figures.name: Experimental Jetset
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Danny van den Dungen, Marieke Stolk, Erwin Brinkers)
figures.summary: Amsterdam trio who fused Dutch modernism with post-punk attitude, using Helvetica, black, white, red and blue as a critical, not corporate, language.

principles.name: Restricted means
principles.idea: Typography alone, mostly Helvetica, in black, white, red and blue: the limits are the identity.

principles.name: Modernism plus punk
principles.idea: De Stijl and Provo are read through Sonic Youth: modernism as an attitude of making, not a corporate look.
principles.example: Studio name, after Sonic Youth's Experimental Jet Set, Trash and No Star (1994), 1997

principles.name: A line that responds
principles.idea: An identity is a single rule that scales to whatever format it lands in.

keyWorks.title: Statement and Counter-Statement: Notes on Experimental Jetset

figures.name: Irma Boom
figures.summary: Amsterdam book designer who builds books as architecture: 2,136 pages without page numbers, inkless embossed pages, sawn edges.

principles.name: Build the book
principles.idea: Thickness, edges, scale and binding carry the content; she works out each book first as a tiny model.

principles.name: Remove the expected
principles.idea: No page numbers, no index, a blank cover, reverse chronology, so the reader discovers rather than navigates.

principles.name: Address other senses
principles.idea: Embossing without ink or frayed edges speak to touch where print would speak to sight.

keyWorks.title: Irma Boom: The Architecture of the Book

figures.name: Vaughan Oliver
figures.summary: 4AD's designer (23 Envelope, then v23), whose surreal, tactile photography and ornate type gave a whole record label one atmosphere.

principles.name: Label as one atmosphere
principles.idea: Different bands share one visual sensibility, so the label itself becomes the brand.

principles.name: Continuity with a fresh approach
principles.idea: Each release of a band's catalogue is new but recognisably part of a series.

principles.name: Texture and the uncanny
principles.idea: Close-up photography, blur and surreal objects make the image felt before it is understood.

keyWorks.title: This Mortal Coil, It'll End in Tears

figures.name: Why Not Associates
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Andy Altmann, David Ellis)
figures.summary: London studio that took 1980s experimental typography into motion, exhibitions and public space, ending up with type you can walk on.

principles.name: Type at architectural scale
principles.idea: Typography leaves the page and becomes floor, wall and landscape, readable from close up and from a tower.
principles.example: Comedy Carpet, Blackpool, with Gordon Young, 2011

principles.name: Experiment for clients
principles.idea: Layered, kinetic typography is applied to commissions rather than kept to self-initiated work.

figures.name: The Designers Republic
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Ian Anderson, Nick Phillips)
figures.summary: Sheffield studio that parodied corporate identity and consumerism for Warp Records, Pop Will Eat Itself and the Wipeout games.

principles.name: Brand the anti-brand
principles.idea: Corporate logos, slogans and fake company names are turned on consumerism itself.
principles.example: 'Work Buy Consume Die' slogans; Pho-Ku corporation, 1990s

principles.name: Maximum-minimalism
principles.idea: Clean, technical layouts are overloaded with icons, codes, anime and tiny type until restraint becomes excess.

principles.name: North of Nowhere
principles.idea: Regional pride (Sheffield, 'SoYo') against the London design scene is part of the voice.

keyWorks.title: Pop Will Eat Itself, Very Metal Noise Pollution

figures.name: Ken Garland
figures.summary: British designer and writer whose 1964 First Things First manifesto asked designers to put their skills to useful work; its 1999 reissue reopened the debate.

principles.name: First things first
principles.idea: Design skill belongs first to useful communication (signs, books, education, science), not to the 'high pitched scream' of consumer selling.

principles.name: Clear form for a cause
principles.idea: Plain, bold modernist graphics serve campaigns and education as well as clients.
principles.example: CND Aldermaston to London Easter march poster, 1962

principles.name: Work is a team effort
principles.idea: He insisted his studio's work was collective, and later argued for partnership with clients over 'us and them'.

figures.name: Norm
figures.role: Graphic and type design studio (Dimitri Bruni, Manuel Krebs)
figures.summary: Zurich duo who rebuilt Swiss modernism from its rules, producing strict, slightly strange typefaces such as Simple and Replica for Lineto.

principles.name: Rules generate form
principles.idea: A typeface comes from a stated construction system, so its oddities are the system's, not the hand's.

principles.name: Modernism with a wink
principles.idea: Strict, rigorous Swiss method with slight references to postmodern play.

events.label: Letraset dry-transfer lettering
events.note: Rub-down letters put display type in anyone's hands, the tool of choice for punk fanzines and the vernacular postmodernists.

events.label: First Things First manifesto
events.note: Ken Garland's manifesto asked designers to prefer useful communication to consumer advertising, a question every later generation reopened.

events.label: Summer of Love
events.note: San Francisco's counterculture turned the dance-hall poster into a national craze and a collectible product.

events.label: International Typeface Corporation founded
events.note: A foundry with no metal-type history, built for photocomposition, whose condensed spacing and big x-heights defined 1970s display type.

events.label: Learning from Las Vegas
events.note: Venturi, Scott Brown and Izenour's book licensed the commercial vernacular as a source, shaping Cranbrook and postmodern graphics.

events.label: Punk's year
events.note: 'God Save the Queen' and Never Mind the Bollocks made cut-up, photocopied graphics a mass-market look.

events.label: Memphis founded in Milan
events.note: Sottsass's group launched postmodern design's loudest attack on functionalist good taste; its first show followed in 1981.

events.label: Apple Macintosh
events.note: A bitmap screen, mouse and fonts on a desk made type and layout a personal, experimental medium; Emigre launched the same year.

events.label: PostScript and the LaserWriter
events.note: Adobe's page-description language made outline type and pages device-independent, the base of desktop publishing.

events.label: Fontographer
events.note: The first commercial Bézier font editor for a personal computer; anyone could now publish a typeface.

events.label: QuarkXPress
events.note: The layout program that dominated professional publishing in the 1990s and made layered, free-form spreads routine.

events.label: Adobe Photoshop 1.0
events.note: Layered raster compositing put photographic collage and texture on every designer's desk, the engine of grunge.

events.label: Vignelli calls Emigre 'garbage'
events.note: Massimo Vignelli's attack in Print made the legibility wars between modernists and the digital avant-garde public.

events.label: Ray Gun launched
events.note: David Carson's art direction took grunge typography from niche to newsstand.

events.label: First Things First 2000 manifesto
events.note: Adbusters, Emigre, Eye and others reissued Garland's manifesto with 33 signatories, reopening the debate about design and consumerism.

events.label: Helvetica documentary
events.note: Gary Hustwit's film, featuring Experimental Jetset and Norm, marked neo-modernism's arrival as a public taste.

events.label: V&A: Postmodernism, Style and Subversion 1970-1990
events.note: The V&A exhibition historicised postmodern design, from Memphis to Emigre, as a closed period.

sources: Philip B. Meggs & Alston W. Purvis, Meggs' History of Graphic Design, 6th ed., 2016
Rick Poynor, No More Rules: Graphic Design and Postmodernism, 2003
Glenn Adamson & Jane Pavitt (eds.), Postmodernism: Style and Subversion 1970-1990, V&A Publishing, 2011
